scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-REFUND-FAIL-COUNT.name: Count of refund submissions failing due to malformed IBAN format

M-MEDIAN-RESPONSE-TIME.name: Median ticket first-response time versus SLA

M-TICKET-REFUND-FAIL-SHARE.name: Share of support tickets attributable to refund-failure follow-ups
M-TICKET-REFUND-FAIL-SHARE.numerator: tickets referencing a refund status/failure matched to a FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT payment-db record

F-01.statement: payment-db.refund_failures returned 5 records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

F-02.statement: ticket-db.response_times reports median_hours=2.0, sla_hours=24, across 900 tickets.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-NO-AUTOMATED-ANSWER-CHANNEL.statement: Customers wait because there is no fast automated channel to get answers; a chatbot answering routine refund-status queries would eliminate the wait.

H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING.statement: The underlying refund payments are slow to process in payment-db, so customers are really waiting for money, not for an answer; a chatbot would only relay delay, not remove it.

H-TICKET-VOLUME-CAPACITY-GAP.statement: Support response delays stem from ticket volume exceeding agent capacity (staffing/triage), not from absence of automation.

H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY.statement: Agents lack integrated visibility across ticket-db and payment-db, so manual cross-system lookups per ticket inflate response times, independent of customer-facing channel.

H-MISSING-PROACTIVE-STATUS-NOT.statement: Customers generate repeat status-check tickets because they are never proactively notified of refund progress, i.e. the root cause is lack of outbound communication, not inbound answer latency.

H-REFUND-IBAN-FAILURE.statement: Refunds are rejected outright due to invalid/malformed IBAN data submitted by customers or upstream systems, and these silent failures drive customers to open support tickets to learn why their refund never arrived.

interpretation_history.interpretation: A direct query of payment-db shows 5 refund_failures records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT — refunds are not merely slow, a subset of them are outright rejected at submission for malformed IBAN data. This points to a data-entry/validation defect in the refund path as a concrete, previously unlisted cause of customer follow-up tickets.

ticket-db reports a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, i.e. the typical ticket is answered well inside SLA. This undercuts the framing that customers are generally waiting a long time for a human answer, which is the premise behind proposing a chatbot to speed up responses.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP (the same stakeholder behind the initial request CL-01) restates, in an interview, that customers wait and a chatbot would answer instantly; this is a non-authoritative reaffirmation of their own response-speed framing (noted bias) rather than new evidence, and adds no data beyond what CL-01 already asserts.

U-CORRELATION.question: Do the FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund failures actually generate a measurable share of the 900 support tickets, or is this a small, separate issue from the main backlog driver?
U-CORRELATION.decision_impact: Determines whether fixing IBAN validation meaningfully reduces ticket volume or whether the backlog has another dominant, still-unidentified driver.
U-CORRELATION.resolution_path: Query ticket-db for tickets referencing refund status/failure and join against payment-db refund IDs with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status.
U-CORRELATION.safe_placeholder: Treat the IBAN fix as a no-regret improvement; do not claim a specific ticket-volume reduction target until correlation is measured.

U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.question: Is the malformed IBAN data entered by the customer at checkout, or produced/corrupted by an upstream system or integration?
U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.decision_impact: Determines whether the fix should be customer-facing input validation versus a backend data-pipeline correction.
U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.resolution_path: Trace a sample of the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records back through the submission pipeline and originating system.
U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.safe_placeholder: Add defensive IBAN validation at the submission point regardless of upstream source as an interim safeguard.

U-NOTIFICATION-GAP.question: Are customers currently notified at all when a refund fails, or do they only discover it by opening a ticket?
U-NOTIFICATION-GAP.decision_impact: Determines whether proactive failure notification should be added alongside the IBAN validation fix.
U-NOTIFICATION-GAP.resolution_path: Check whether payment-db or ticket-db logs any outbound notification event tied to refund failures.
U-NOTIFICATION-GAP.safe_placeholder: Do not assume notification already exists; keep notify_customers_of_refund_failure in scope pending confirmation.

A-FAILURE-TICKET-LINK.statement: The FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund failures are a cause of some of the 900 support tickets, rather than an unrelated, separately-tracked data point.

A-FAILURES-CURRENT.statement: The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records represent current/open failures rather than already-resolved historical ones.

A-SILENT-FAILURE.statement: Customers are not proactively notified when a refund fails with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, so they only learn of it by opening a ticket.

SC-NO-IBAN-FAIL.statement: Eliminate outright refund rejections caused by malformed IBAN format.
SC-NO-IBAN-FAIL.validation_method: Re-run payment-db.refund_failures query and confirm no FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status records remain.

SC-RESPONSE-GUARDRAIL.statement: Do not degrade existing ticket response performance while implementing the fix.
SC-RESPONSE-GUARDRAIL.validation_method: Re-run ticket-db.response_times query post-change and compare median_hours to sla_hours.

SC-TICKET-SHARE-REDUCTION.statement: Reduce the share of support tickets caused by refund-failure follow-ups once a baseline correlation is established.
SC-TICKET-SHARE-REDUCTION.threshold: measurable decrease from established baseline after fix
SC-TICKET-SHARE-REDUCTION.validation_method: Join ticket-db tickets referencing refund issues with payment-db refund IDs before and after the fix and compare share.

VOB-U-CORRELATION.unresolved_question: Do the FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund failures actually generate a measurable share of the 900 support tickets, or is this a small, separate issue from the main backlog driver?
VOB-U-CORRELATION.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Treat the IBAN fix as a no-regret improvement; do not claim a specific ticket-volume reduction target until correlation is measured.
VOB-U-CORRELATION.validation_method: Query ticket-db for tickets referencing refund status/failure and join against payment-db refund IDs with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status.

VOB-U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.unresolved_question: Is the malformed IBAN data entered by the customer at checkout, or produced/corrupted by an upstream system or integration?
VOB-U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Add defensive IBAN validation at the submission point regardless of upstream source as an interim safeguard.
VOB-U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN.validation_method: Trace a sample of the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records back through the submission pipeline and originating system.

VOB-R-3.unresolved_question: Are customers currently notified at all when a refund fails, or do they only discover it by opening a ticket? (U-NOTIFICATION-GAP)
VOB-R-3.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-11: Building a new notification feature without confirming whether one already exists risks duplicate effort or masking an already-broken channel, mirroring how VOB-U-CORRELATION and VOB-U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN already gate the other remedies.
VOB-R-3.validation_method: Check payment-db/ticket-db or existing notification/alerting logs for evidence of outbound refund-failure messages before building a new notification feature.
required_evidence: Log or record showing presence/absence of existing outbound refund-failure notifications to customers

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds (SH-SUP, CL-01).
symptoms: Support lead reports customers wait for refund answers and requests a chatbot (CL-01; E-03 restates the same framing).
payment-db.refund_failures shows 5 records, all status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
ticket-db.response_times shows median_hours=2.0 against sla_hours=24 across 900 tickets, i.e. responses are already fast (E-02).
problem_definition.root_problem: Support tickets framed by the requester as a response-speed backlog are, in a documented subset of cases, actually driven by refunds that fail outright at submission due to malformed IBAN data (5 payment-db records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), causing customers to open tickets to find out why their refund never arrived; meanwhile median ticket response time (2.0h) is already well within the 24h SLA across 900 tickets, ruling out slow/absent answering as the mechanism.

structural_remedies.rationale: Only 5 records, small remediation, but execution is a write action and payment-db is read-only in this session; requires handoff.; residual gap: Clears only existing 5 cases; without R1 the failure mode recurs for future refunds.

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Refund submissions carry malformed/invalid IBAN data (E-01). → payment-db rejects these submissions outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT; 5 such records found (E-01). → The refund never completes and the customer receives no money, with no confirmed proactive notice of the failure (interpretation of E-01). → Lacking an explanation, the customer opens a support ticket to ask about the missing/undelivered refund, contributing to perceived backlog (CL-01 framing). → Ticket response speed is not the actual bottleneck, since median first response (2.0h) is well inside the 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), which rules out 'no automated answer channel' as the driving mechanism.; rejected framings: [('H-NO-AUTOMATED-ANSWER-CHANNEL', 'Contradicted by E-01 (customers face outright refund rejections, not mere wait-for-answer latency) and E-02 (median response time 2.0h is well within the 24h SLA); only supported by E-03, a non-authoritative restatement by the same biased requester as CL-01.'), ('H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING', 'Contradicted by E-01, which shows outright rejection with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT rather than merely slow processing.'), ('H-TICKET-VOLUME-CAPACITY-GAP', 'Contradicted by E-02, which shows response times well within SLA, indicating agent capacity is not the limiting factor.'), ('H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY', 'Status REJECTED and contradicted by E-02 showing fast median response times, so cross-system lookup delay is not supported as a driver.')]
[CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-CORRELATION deferred to VOB-U-CORRELATION; [CONDITIONAL] critical unknown U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN deferred to VOB-U-ROOT-CAUSE-IBAN

framing_assertion.value: lack of an automated chatbot answer channel causes customers to wait for refund information
framing_assertion.rationale: SH-SUP (support lead, flagged bias: 'frames everything as response speed') requests a chatbot to stop customers 'waiting for answers about refunds', asserting the root cause is answer-channel latency rather than any upstream process issue.

hypotheses.statement: Customers wait because there is no fast automated channel to get answers; a chatbot answering routine refund-status queries would eliminate the wait.
hypotheses.rationale: This is SH-SUP's stated justification for the chatbot ask; if true the chatbot build is the correct fix, but SH-SUP's noted bias toward framing everything as response speed means it must be tested, not assumed.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db response times segmented by query type (status-check vs other)
DA-TCK completeness/authority on whether tickets are simple lookups

hypotheses.statement: The underlying refund payments are slow to process in payment-db, so customers are really waiting for money, not for an answer; a chatbot would only relay delay, not remove it.
hypotheses.rationale: If refunds themselves are backlogged, a chatbot cannot shorten customer wait time and the real fix is in the refund (P-REF) process, making the requested solution ineffective.
discriminating_evidence: correlation between refund processing duration and ticket creation timestamps in DA-TCK

hypotheses.statement: Support response delays stem from ticket volume exceeding agent capacity (staffing/triage), not from absence of automation.
hypotheses.rationale: If the bottleneck is capacity rather than query complexity, the fix is staffing or triage prioritization, and a chatbot may only deflect low-value tickets while leaving the capacity gap unresolved.
discriminating_evidence: ticket-db response time distribution relative to ticket inflow rate

hypotheses.statement: Agents lack integrated visibility across ticket-db and payment-db, so manual cross-system lookups per ticket inflate response times, independent of customer-facing channel.
hypotheses.rationale: If the delay is internal (agents manually reconciling DA-TCK and DA-PAY), the fix is internal tooling/integration rather than a customer-facing chatbot.
discriminating_evidence: time-per-ticket breakdown showing manual lookup steps
whether DA-PAY and DA-TCK are queried separately per ticket resolution

actions.question: What is the current rate and pattern of refund failures/delays in payment-db, and do refund processing times correlate with ticket backlog spikes?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether refund processing itself is slow/failing, which would show customers are waiting on money movement rather than information, directly testing the CRITICAL-impact hypothesis.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING has CRITICAL decision_impact; if confirmed, a chatbot (the requested solution) would not address root cause, changing the recommended next action entirely.
actions.why_now: This catalog item's refund_failures operation most directly names the exact mechanism (slow/failing refund payment processing) claimed by H-SLOW-REFUND-PROCESSING, which is still CANDIDATE and carries the highest decision_impact among live hypotheses.

actions.question: What do ticket response-time distributions, ticket volumes over time, and repeat-contact rates in ticket-db show about the causes of the backlog?
actions.expected_information_gain: Volume-vs-capacity patterns would support/reject H-TICKET-VOLUME-CAPACITY-GAP; repeat status-check tickets would support H-MISSING-PROACTIVE-STATUS-NOT and H-NO-AUTOMATED-ANSWER-CHANNEL; slow per-ticket handle times could point to H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: These are the three remaining live hypotheses with HIGH/MEDIUM decision_impact whose mechanism (ticket pattern) is directly observable only via this ticket-db query; result would change whether chatbot, staffing, proactive-notification, or tooling-integration is pursued.
actions.why_now: This is the only catalog item describing ticket response-time and volume data, the exact mechanism named by four still-CANDIDATE hypotheses about capacity, proactive notification, automated channel, and lookup delay.

actions.question: Ask the support lead to describe current agent workflow: do agents manually cross-reference ticket-db and payment-db per ticket, and is CL-01's framing (customers waiting for answers) based on observed agent pain points or assumption?
actions.expected_information_gain: Could confirm or disconfirm whether agents actually perform manual cross-system lookups (the mechanism H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY claims), which no system-data query directly observes.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY's mechanism (lack of integrated visibility) is a workflow fact not captured by either data system, so only the stakeholder closest to agent operations can speak to it, though their known bias toward 'response speed' framing limits reliability.
actions.why_now: This is the only catalog item that could surface agent-workflow/lookup-silo information, the mechanism H-AGENT-DATA-SILO-LOOKUP-DELAY names, since neither remaining tool query observes agent process steps directly.

proposal.interpretation: A direct query of payment-db shows 5 refund_failures records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT — refunds are not merely slow, a subset of them are outright rejected at submission for malformed IBAN data. This points to a data-entry/validation defect in the refund path as a concrete, previously unlisted cause of customer follow-up tickets.

hypothesis_effects.rationale: The observed failures are categorical rejections (FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), not instances of processing taking longer than usual, so the 'slow processing' causal story does not match this failure mode.
If refunds are failing due to invalid IBAN format, a chatbot answering status queries would only relay the failure, not resolve it, so the wait is not purely an answer-latency problem.
Silent IBAN-format failures are consistent with customers not being proactively told their refund failed, prompting them to open tickets to find out what happened.
This observation says nothing about agent staffing or ticket volume relative to capacity.
The observation does not speak to whether agents can cross-reference ticket-db and payment-db manually.

payment-db rejects these submissions outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT; 5 such records found (E-01).
The refund never completes and the customer receives no money, with no confirmed proactive notice of the failure (interpretation of E-01).

Ticket response speed is not the actual bottleneck, since median first response (2.0h) is well inside the 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), which rules out 'no automated answer channel' as the driving mechanism.

Only 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records are known (F-01), and ticket-db completeness (DA-TCK) is UNKNOWN, so broader scope could change the picture.
Whether the 5 known failures are current/open or already-resolved historical cases is an unverified assumption (A-FAILURES-CURRENT), not confirmed by evidence.

It is not established whether customers are currently notified when a refund fails or only discover it by opening a ticket (U-NOTIFICATION-GAP / VOB-R-3), which affects the notify_customers_of_refund_failure action in scope.
No mutating tools were available this session (payment-db and ticket-db are read-only), so the retry and notification actions cannot be executed now and must be handed off for execution.
